summary.text: Take \(n=2^{14}\cdot4409\cdot458009=33085221781504\), where \(4409\) and \(458009\) are distinct odd primes. Using multiplicativity together with \(\sigma(2^k)=2^{k+1}-1\), \(\sum_{d\mid 2^k}\sigma(d)=2^{k+2}-k-3\), and \(\sum_{d\mid p}\sigma(d)=p+2\) for prime \(p\), one obtains \(a(n)=2(32767\cdot4410\cdot458010)-(65519\cdot4411\cdot458011)=1\), although \(n\ne1,12\).

full_proof.text:
Let \(\sigma(m)=\sum_{e\mid m}e\) denote the sum of the positive divisors of \(m\). The deficiency of \(m\) is
\[
\delta(m)=m-\sum_{\substack{e\mid m\\e<m}}e=2m-\sigma(m).
\]
Thus the sequence in question is
\[
a(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\delta(d)=\sum_{d\mid n}\bigl(2d-\sigma(d)\bigr),
\]
where the sum is taken in the integers, since deficiencies can be negative.

We will exhibit the counterexample
\[
N=2^{14}\cdot 4409\cdot 458009=33{,}085{,}221{,}781{,}504.
\]
We prove directly that \(a(N)=1\).

Define the auxiliary function
\[
B(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\sigma(d).
\]
Because \(\sum_{d\mid n}d=\sigma(n)\), summing the expression for the deficiency gives the useful identity
\[
\boxed{a(n)=2\sigma(n)-B(n).}\tag{1}
\]

Both \(\sigma\) and \(B\) are multiplicative. More explicitly, if \(m\) and \(n\) are coprime, every divisor of \(mn\) has a unique expression \(ef\), with \(e\mid m\) and \(f\mid n\), and \(e,f\) are coprime. The same unique decomposition of divisors shows that
\[
\sigma(ef)=\sigma(e)\sigma(f)
\]
when \(e\) and \(f\) are coprime. Consequently,
\[
\sigma(mn)=\sigma(m)\sigma(n).
\]
Using the divisor decomposition once more,
\[
\begin{aligned}
B(mn)
 &=\sum_{e\mid m}\sum_{f\mid n}\sigma(ef)\\
 &=\sum_{e\mid m}\sum_{f\mid n}\sigma(e)\sigma(f)\\
 &=B(m)B(n).
\end{aligned}\tag{2}
\]

We next evaluate these functions on the factors of \(N\). If \(p\) is prime, its divisors are \(1,p\), so
\[
\sigma(p)=p+1
\quad\text{and}\quad
B(p)=\sigma(1)+\sigma(p)=1+(p+1)=p+2.\tag{3}
\]
For a power of two, the divisors of \(2^k\) are \(1,2,\ldots,2^k\). Hence
\[
\sigma(2^k)=1+2+\cdots+2^k=2^{k+1}-1.\tag{4}
\]
Also,
\[
\begin{aligned}
B(2^k)
 &=\sum_{j=0}^k\sigma(2^j)\\
 &=\sum_{j=0}^k(2^{j+1}-1)\\
 &=\left(2+4+\cdots+2^{k+1}\right)-(k+1)\\
 &=\bigl(2^{k+2}-2\bigr)-(k+1)\\
 &=2^{k+2}-k-3.
\end{aligned}\tag{5}
\]
In particular, at \(k=14\),
\[
\sigma(2^{14})=2^{15}-1=32767,
\qquad
B(2^{14})=2^{16}-14-3=65519.\tag{6}
\]

For completeness, we now justify the primality of the two odd factors used in \(N\). The following standard elementary primality criterion gives a compact way to record all the required finite computations.

**Lucas primality criterion.** Suppose the complete prime factorization of \(n-1\) is known. If there is an integer \(g\) such that
\[
g^{n-1}\equiv1\pmod n
\]
and, for every distinct prime \(q\mid n-1\),
\[
\gcd\left(g^{(n-1)/q}-1,n\right)=1,
\]
then \(n\) is prime.

Indeed, let \(r\) be any prime divisor of \(n\). The first congruence ensures that \(g\) is nonzero modulo \(r\), and the multiplicative order of \(g\) modulo \(r\) divides \(n-1\). The gcd conditions say that, for every prime \(q\mid n-1\), this order does not divide \((n-1)/q\). It follows that the order contains every prime power occurring in \(n-1\), and therefore the order is exactly \(n-1\). By Fermat's theorem the order also divides \(r-1\), so \(n-1\le r-1\), or \(r\ge n\). Since \(r\mid n\), this forces \(r=n\), proving that \(n\) is prime.

Here is a recursive Lucas certificate for all primes needed below. In each row, the displayed factorization is that of \(n-1\); the entry \(q:r\) means
\[
g^{(n-1)/q}\equiv r\pmod n.
\]
Repeated squaring gives \(g^{n-1}\equiv1\pmod n\) in every row, and the final column records that \(\gcd(r-1,n)=1\) for every listed residue. Only the distinct prime divisors \(q\) of \(n-1\) need to be listed.

\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c}
 n & n-1 & g & q:r & \gcd(r-1,n)\\ \hline
3 & 2 & 2 & 2:2 & 1\\
5 & 2^2 & 2 & 2:4 & 1\\
7 & 2\cdot3 & 3 & 2:6,\ 3:2 & 1,1\\
19 & 2\cdot3^2 & 2 & 2:18,\ 3:7 & 1,1\\
29 & 2^2\cdot7 & 2 & 2:28,\ 7:16 & 1,1\\
229 & 2^2\cdot3\cdot19 & 6 & 2:228,\ 3:134,\ 19:165 & 1,1,1\\
57251 & 2\cdot5^3\cdot229 & 2 & 2:57250,\ 5:55371,\ 229:48088 & 1,1,1\\
4409 & 2^3\cdot19\cdot29 & 3 & 2:4408,\ 19:209,\ 29:3965 & 1,1,1\\
458009 & 2^3\cdot57251 & 3 & 2:458008,\ 57251:6561 & 1,1
\end{array}
\]

For clarity, the gcd assertions in the last two rows are
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\gcd(4407,4409)=\gcd(208,4409)=\gcd(3964,4409)=1,\\
&\gcd(458007,458009)=\gcd(6560,458009)=1,
\end{aligned}
\]
and similarly the residues in each earlier row give the displayed gcds. All entries are ordinary modular exponentiations and Euclidean-algorithm computations. Starting with the evident primality of \(2\), the rows successively establish the primality of every prime appearing in the factorization used by a later row. Thus, in particular, both \(4409\) and \(458009\) are prime.

These are distinct odd primes, so \(2^{14}\), \(4409\), and \(458009\) are pairwise coprime. We may therefore apply multiplicativity (2), together with (3) and (6). For the divisor-sum function,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sigma(N)
 &=\sigma(2^{14})\sigma(4409)\sigma(458009)\\
 &=32767\cdot4410\cdot458010.
\end{aligned}\tag{7}
\]
For the auxiliary function,
\[
\begin{aligned}
B(N)
 &=B(2^{14})B(4409)B(458009)\\
 &=65519\cdot4411\cdot458011.
\end{aligned}\tag{8}
\]
Substitution into (1) now gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(N)
 &=2\cdot32767\cdot4410\cdot458010
   -65519\cdot4411\cdot458011.
\end{aligned}
\]
The two products are
\[
2\cdot32767\cdot4410\cdot458010
 =132{,}367{,}152{,}569{,}400
\]
and
\[
65519\cdot4411\cdot458011
 =132{,}367{,}152{,}569{,}399.
\]
Their difference is therefore exactly
\[
\boxed{a(N)=1}.
\]

Finally,
\[
N=33{,}085{,}221{,}781{,}504>12,
\]
so \(N\) is neither \(1\) nor \(12\). Thus there is a positive integer other than \(1\) and \(12\) at which the sum of the deficiencies of the divisors is \(1\). This counterexample disproves the conjectured equivalence
\[
a(n)=1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad n=1\text{ or }n=12.
\]
